title: The Unwise Schoolmaster

full_text:
In a village near Damascus lived a schoolmaster who was deeply versed in ancient grammatical rules, archaic vocabulary, and obsolete legal commentaries, but who possessed not a single grain of ordinary common sense. He insisted on speaking in ancient rhetorical verses even when ordering onions in the marketplace, causing confusion wherever he went.

One afternoon, the schoolmaster was riding his donkey along a narrow canal path, engrossed in reading a massive leather-bound dictionary held before his nose. The donkey, left to its own judgment, wandered off the path, and both beast and master tumbled into a deep ditch filled with black mud.

A passing farmer saw the mishap, ran up with a long willow pole, and shouted: 'Catch hold of the pole, master, and I will pull you out of the ditch!'

The schoolmaster, covered in black slime up to his chin, looked up haughtily and replied in high classical rhetoric: 'O rustic agriculturalist! Thou hast addressed me with a grammatical solecism! Thou shouldst have exclaimed: "Grasp thou the extremity of the arboreal branch, that I may extract thy physical vessel from the alluvial mire!" Correct thy syntax immediately, before I deign to accept thy assistance!'

The farmer blinked in astonishment, shrugged his shoulders, and said: 'If you prefer grammar to dry clothes, master, stay in the mud and conjugate your verbs!' The farmer picked up his pole and walked away.

The schoolmaster spent three hours struggling in the slimy ditch, ruining his precious dictionary and catching a severe chill, before a passing cart driver hauled him out without asking for his grammatical approval.

The drenched pedagogue returned home shivering, having learned that in the hour of difficulty, a plain word spoken with practical sense is worth more than ten thousand archaic dictionaries.
moral: Pedantic knowledge that lacks practical common sense makes a man a laughingstock to his neighbors.
